analysis.one_liner: Bases seniors' Medicare drug coinsurance on the drug's actual discounted price, not the higher list price.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would lower some seniors' Medicare drug coinsurance, has not moved since being referred to two House committees in February 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Under Medicare's prescription drug benefit, some seniors pay a percentage of a drug's price as coinsurance. Plans often calculate that share off the drug's wholesale list price, which is higher than what the plan actually pays after manufacturer discounts and rebates. This bill would require the coinsurance share to be based on the lower, actual price the plan pays, when that price is lower, starting with plan year 2026.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D enrollees whose plans charge percentage coinsurance on drugs, mainly brand-name drugs, in the portion of the year after the deductible and before the annual out-of-pocket maximum. They would owe a smaller coinsurance amount on drugs where the plan's real cost, after manufacturer concessions, is below the list price.

how_it_helps.text: Requires that coinsurance for covered Part D drugs be calculated from the drug's actual acquisition cost, the negotiated plan price net of manufacturer price concessions, whenever that is lower than the wholesale acquisition cost [S2][S3].

Applies to plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, for costs between the annual deductible and the annual out-of-pocket threshold, for drugs subject to coinsurance rather than a flat copayment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Part D plans would collect less in coinsurance from enrollees and would bear more of each covered drug's cost themselves, a cost that could be recovered through higher premiums. Drugmakers' list prices would still exist, but their discounted prices would directly set the enrollee's share.
analysis.who_pays_short: Part D plans and, possibly, all enrollees

drawbacks.text: The savings only reach seniors in the band between the deductible and the out-of-pocket threshold, and only on drugs charged as percentage coinsurance rather than a flat copay; drugs in certain excluded categories are carved out [S3].

The bill shifts the difference between list and net prices from enrollees to plans. Plans could recoup that through higher premiums, spreading the cost to all Part D enrollees including those who take no coinsurance drugs; the bill contains no mechanism addressing premium effects.
The net price is taken from plan-submitted reports on manufacturer concessions, so accuracy depends on plans reporting those concessions correctly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors on plans that set coinsurance off the higher list price, the bill delivers a real, direct cut in what they pay at the pharmacy. The cost is diffuse: plans may pass the shift on through premiums, so some of the savings could be offset for the broader enrollee pool. The design is narrow but straightforward, and its main weakness is how little ground it covers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, and no committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Davis introduced the bill on February 12, 2025, joined by Rep. August Pfluger as its only cosponsor at introduction [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee [S5].
The action history shows no further activity, no hearing, markup, or floor vote, since the February 2025 referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo holds: Part D plans can continue setting enrollee coinsurance off the higher wholesale list price rather than the net price they actually pay.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Plans keeping the current coinsurance formula

for.name: Rep. Donald G. Davis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to base Part D coinsurance on the drug's actual acquisition cost.

for.name: Rep. August Pfluger
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor, the bill's only cosponsor listed.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.role: Committees with jurisdiction over Medicare drug benefit provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in February 2025 and have taken no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is bipartisan, one House Democrat and one House Republican, but with only two cosponsors total there is no organized bloc on either side and no vote record to measure party splits.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and plan sponsors
industries.note: Plans can currently set the enrollee's percentage coinsurance off the higher wholesale list price, collecting more from seniors than the drug's real cost reflects. The bill would cap that share at the net price, cutting enrollee costs at plans' expense, though plans may shift the difference into premiums.

The bill does not touch the rebate-and-concession system PBMs run; it defines the new coinsurance base as the negotiated price net of manufacturer concessions reported through existing plan filings. It accepts that structure as the source of the lower price rather than replacing it.

Manufacturers keep list prices and continue paying concessions, but those concessions would now directly lower what seniors owe instead of being absorbed in the middle of the supply chain. That reduces the value of maintaining a wide gap between list and net prices.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat in two committees since its February 2025 referral with no hearing, markup, or vote, and only two cosponsors. Bills at this stage in this position rarely reach the floor; unless a committee schedules it or leadership attaches it to a larger Medicare package, it is likely to die at the end of this Congress without a vote.
